Second-largest branch of [[Islam]], defined by the belief that [[Muhammad]] designated his cousin and son-in-law [[Ali|Ali ibn Abi Talib]] (r. 656–661) as his successor.

Shia Muslims hold that Ali was the rightful political successor (caliph) and the divinely guided spiritual leader (imam) of the Muslim community. They maintain that his right was unjustly usurped at the meeting of Saqifa, where [[Abu Bakr]] (r. 632–634) was chosen as caliph. Sunni Muslims accept the rule of Abu Bakr, [[Umar]] (r. 634–644), and [[Uthman]] (r. 644–656). Shia sources cite Muhammad's sermon at Ghadir Khumm, "Anyone who has me as his mawla, has Ali as his mawla"; Sunni scholars tend to read it as a general affirmation of Ali's merit, while Shia Muslims regard it as a clear designation. The Shia first emerged as a distinct movement during the First Fitna (656–661). Scholars debate their origins: some Western historians describe early Shia Islam as merely a political faction, while others call that view an anachronistic imposition of a Western separation of religion and politics.

Shia Muslims believe the imamate continued through Ali's sons, Hasan and Husayn, after whom various branches emerged. Central to Shia devotion is reverence for the ahl al-bayt, the family of Muhammad, regarded as infallible inheritors of his knowledge and spiritual authority. Holy sites include the shrine of Ali in Najaf and that of Husayn in Karbala, and mourning rituals commemorate Husayn's death at Karbala in 680. The three principal branches are Twelverism, Isma'ilism, and Zaydism. Twelvers, estimated at 85–90% of Shia Muslims, hold that twelve imams succeeded Ali, the last entering occultation in 874. Historical Shia states include the [[Fatimid Caliphate]] (909–1171).

Shia Muslims are estimated at 10–13% of the world's Muslims, roughly 200–260 million. They form a majority in [[Iran]], Iraq, and Azerbaijan and almost half the Muslim population of Lebanon and Bahrain. Iran is the only country where Shia Islam officially underlies both the legal framework and the system of governance.

Religion of [[Japan]] centered on the veneration of kami, supernatural entities believed to inhabit all things.

Classified as an East Asian religion by scholars, Shinto is often regarded by its practitioners as Japan's indigenous religion and as a nature religion. It has no central authority, single creator, or specific doctrine, and exists in diverse local and regional forms. The kami, who include forces of nature and prominent landscape locations, are worshipped at household shrines (kamidana), family shrines, and public shrines (jinja). Priests called kannushi staff the public shrines and oversee offerings of food and drink, intended to cultivate harmony between humans and kami and to solicit their blessing. Other common rituals include kagura dances, rites of passage, and kami festivals; shrines also offer [[Divination|divination]] and supply amulets. Purity is a major concern, pursued through ritual washing and bathing. Little emphasis falls on specific moral codes or afterlife beliefs, although the dead can become kami. The emperor's descent from [[Amaterasu]] is a longstanding tradition.

Historians debate when it is suitable to speak of Shinto as a distinct religion. Kami veneration has been traced to Japan's Yayoi period (300 BC–AD 250). [[Buddhism]] entered Japan at the end of the Kofun period and spread rapidly; the two became functionally inseparable in a process called shinbutsu-shūgō. The earliest written tradition of kami worship appears in the 8th-century [[Kojiki]] and *Nihon Shoki*. During the Meiji era (1868–1912), nationalist leaders expelled Buddhist influence and formed State Shinto, which some historians regard as the origin of Shinto as a distinct religion; citizens were encouraged to worship the emperor as a kami. With the [[Empire of Japan]], Shinto was exported to other parts of East Asia. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II|World War II]], it was formally separated from the state.

Shinto is numerically Japan's largest religion, with Buddhism second. Most of the population takes part in both Shinto and Buddhist activities, especially festivals. Aspects of Shinto have been incorporated into various [[New religious movement|new religious movements]].

Large watercraft designed for travel across the surface of a body of water, carrying cargo or passengers, or supporting specialized tasks such as warfare, oceanography, and fishing.

Ships are generally distinguished from [[Boat|boats]] by size, shape, load capacity, and purpose, but there is no universally accepted distinction. Ships can typically remain at sea longer than boats, and a common notion holds that a ship can carry a boat but not the reverse. Some large vessels are traditionally called boats, notably [[Submarine|submarines]]. The word has meant either simply a large vessel or, from the mid-18th century, specifically a full-rigged ship with three or more masts, all square-rigged. "Ship" retains a female grammatical gender in some usages; by 2019, Lloyd's Register switched to calling ships "it".

The earliest historical evidence of boats is found in Egypt in the 4th millennium BC. Model ships from [[Mesopotamia]] date to the same millennium. The [[Austronesian peoples]], who originated in what is now [[Taiwan]], developed catamarans, outriggers, and crab claw sails, and spread across Maritime Southeast Asia to Micronesia, Island Melanesia, Polynesia, and [[Madagascar]]. For most of history, transport by ship was cheaper, safer, and faster than overland travel, a principle changed only by railways in the mid-19th century and commercial aviation in the second half of the 20th. A sailing ship of the Roman Empire could carry grain the length of the Mediterranean for less than it cost to move the same amount 15 miles by road, and Rome consumed about 150,000 tons of Egyptian grain a year in the first three centuries AD.

Ships have supported exploration, trade, warfare, migration, colonization, and science, and ship transport carries the largest portion of world commerce. In 2024, ships had a global cargo capacity of 2.4 billion tons; the three largest classes were dry bulk carriers (43%), [[Tanker (ship)|oil tankers]] (28%), and container ships (14%).

Brief work of narrative fiction in [[Prose|prose]] that can typically be read in a single sitting.

A short story focuses on a self-contained incident or a series of linked incidents, intended to evoke a single effect or mood. It uses plot and other components found in the [[Novel|novel]], but typically to a lesser degree. Defining it remains problematic. [[Edgar Allan Poe]]'s essay "The Philosophy of Composition" (1846) made the classic point that it should be readable in one sitting, and H. G. Wells said it should take from fifteen to fifty minutes to read aloud. Somerset Maugham held that a story must have a plot, while [[Anton Chekhov]] thought it should have neither a beginning nor an end but be a suggestive "slice of life". [[William Faulkner]] saw it as character-driven. Typical length is 1,000 to 4,000 words, though some works classified as short stories reach 15,000; stories under 1,000 words are called "short short stories" or flash fiction. The Science Fiction and Fantasy Writers of America defines a short story for the Nebula Awards as fewer than 7,500 words. Longer stories that are not novels are called novellas or novelettes.

The form descends from oral storytelling traditions that produced epics such as the *Ramayana*, the *Mahabharata*, and Homer's *Iliad* and *Odyssey*, and it has existed as legends, myths, folk tales, fairy tales, fables, and anecdotes in many ancient communities. The anecdote, a brief realistic narrative that embodies a point, was popular during the [[Roman Empire]]; many surviving examples were collected in the 13th or 14th century as the *Gesta Romanorum*. In Europe, oral storytelling began to develop into written form in the early 14th century, most notably with [[Giovanni Boccaccio]]'s *Decameron* and [[Geoffrey Chaucer]]'s *Canterbury Tales*.

The modern short story developed in the early 19th century, and the term acquired its modern meaning in the 1880s, having initially referred to children's tales. Writers such as Washington Irving, Nathaniel Hawthorne, Nikolai Gogol, and Guy de Maupassant shaped it, and in the 20th century it underwent expansive experimentation. Its evolution has been closely tied to the publishing industry.

Austrian neurologist, founder of [[Psychoanalysis]].

Born Sigismund Schlomo Freud to Ashkenazi Jewish parents in Freiberg, Moravia, in the Austrian Empire (now Příbor, Czech Republic), he grew up in Vienna after his family moved there in 1860. He entered the [[University of Vienna]] in 1873 at age 17 and graduated with an MD in March 1881. His early research, in Ernst Brücke's physiology laboratory, compared the brains of humans with those of other animals and proved seminal for the discovery of the [[Neuron|neuron]] in the 1890s.

Psychoanalysis is a clinical method for treating pathologies arising from conflicts in the psyche through dialogue between patient and analyst. Freud introduced free association, the interpretation of dreams, and the analysis of transference. His redefinition of sexuality to include infantile stages led him to formulate the [[Oedipus complex]] as a central tenet. He analyzed dreams as wish fulfillments, which gave him models for understanding symptom formation and repression, and on this basis he elaborated a theory of the unconscious and a model of psychic structure comprising id, ego, and superego. He also postulated libido, a sexualized psychic energy, and a death drive, which he saw as the source of compulsive repetition, hate, aggression, and neurotic guilt. His later work offered a wide-ranging interpretation and critique of religion and culture. He emigrated to London in 1938 amid Nazi persecution.

Though less prevalent in diagnostic and clinical practice, psychoanalysis remains influential within [[Psychology|psychology]], [[Psychiatry|psychiatry]], psychotherapy, and the [[Humanities|humanities]]. It continues to generate debate over its therapeutic efficacy, its scientific status, and whether it advances or hinders the feminist cause. Critics, including philosophers of science, have classified key elements as pseudoscientific because of their reliance on case studies rather than controlled evidence. W. H. Auden's 1940 tribute described Freud as "no more a person now but a whole climate of opinion / under whom we conduct our different lives".

Monotheistic Indian religion and philosophy that originated in the [[Punjab]] region around the end of the 15th century.

Followed by 25–30 million adherents, known as Sikhs, it is one of the most recently founded major religions. It developed from the teachings of [[Guru Nanak]], the first guru, and nine successors. The tenth, [[Guru Gobind Singh]], named the [[Guru Granth Sahib]] as his successor, closing the line of human gurus; Sikhs regard it as the 11th and eternally living guru.

Core beliefs, articulated in the Guru Granth Sahib, include faith in one creator (Ik Onkar), called Waheguru; the divine unity and equality of all humankind; selfless service (sevā); striving for justice for all (sarbat da bhala); and honest conduct and livelihood. Sikhism is described as monotheistic and panentheistic, and holds that God is without gender in a literal sense. It rejects claims that any one tradition has a monopoly on absolute truth, so Sikhs do not actively proselytise, though voluntary converts are generally accepted. [[Meditation]] and remembrance of God (simran) are expressed through devotional music (kirtan) or inwardly through naam japna. The Gurus taught that worldly illusion (māyā) and the "Five Thieves" of ego, anger, greed, attachment, and lust distract from devotion. Sikhs emphasise the congruence of spiritual development and everyday moral conduct; Guru Nanak said, "Truth is the highest virtue, but higher still is truthful living."

The religion developed in times of religious persecution and gained converts from both [[Hinduism]] and [[Islam]]. The Mughal emperors tortured and executed two gurus, Guru Arjan and Guru Tegh Bahadur, after they refused to convert to Islam. In response to persecution, Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa in 1699, an order to protect freedom of conscience and religion whose members embody the ideal of the sant-sipāhī ("saint-soldier"). Baptised Sikhs wear the five Ks, articles of faith that include kesh (uncut hair), which is why most religious Sikh men wear a turban. Some Sikhs prefer the term Sikhi to Sikhism, arguing that an "-ism" implies a fixed worldview.

[[Chemical element]] (symbol Si, atomic number 14), a hard, brittle crystalline solid with a blue-grey metallic lustre.

A tetravalent non-metal (sometimes considered a metalloid) and [[Semiconductor|semiconductor]], silicon belongs to group 14 of the periodic table, below carbon, and is relatively unreactive. It melts at 1414 °C and boils at 3265 °C, the second highest values among the metalloids and nonmetals after boron. Its density is 2.329 g/cm³, and natural silicon is a mixture of three stable isotopes: ²⁸Si (92.2%), ²⁹Si (4.7%), and ³⁰Si (3.1%). It is the eighth most common element in the universe by mass and, at about 28% by mass, the second most abundant in the Earth's crust after [[Oxygen|oxygen]]. It rarely occurs pure; more than 90% of the crust is composed of [[Silicate|silicate]] minerals.

Because of its high affinity for oxygen, it resisted isolation. Antoine Lavoisier suspected in 1787 that silica was an oxide of an unknown element. Humphry Davy proposed the name "silicium", from Latin *silex*, "flint", believing it a metal; in 1817 Thomas Thomson gave it its present name, adding "-on" because he thought it a nonmetal like boron and carbon. [[Jöns Jacob Berzelius]] is usually credited with the discovery for preparing and purifying amorphous silicon.

Most silicon is used commercially without being separated, as clay, silica sand, and stone in construction, as silicates in Portland cement and [[Concrete|concrete]], and in porcelain and glass. Silicon carbide serves as an abrasive and in high-strength ceramics, and silicon is the basis of the synthetic polymers called [[Silicone|silicones]]. Less than 15% of silicon is highly purified for semiconductor electronics, where it is essential to transistors, solar cells, and [[Integrated circuit|integrated circuit]] chips, so the late 20th and early 21st centuries have been called the Silicon Age. Silicon is essential for several processes in plants, and sea sponges, diatoms, and radiolaria build skeletal structures of silica.

Network of [[Asia|Asian]] trade routes, active from the second century BC until the mid-15th century, linking East and West.

Spanning over 6,400 km on land, it facilitated economic, cultural, political, and religious exchange. It took its name from the trade in silk textiles produced mainly in China; the term was coined in the late 19th century and popularized in 1877 by Ferdinand von Richthofen. The network began with the expansion of the [[Han dynasty]] into Central Asia around 114 BC, through the missions of the imperial envoy [[Zhang Qian]]. The [[Parthian Empire]] provided a bridge to the Mediterranean, and by the first century AD Chinese silk was widely sought in Rome, Egypt, and Greece. Other goods from the East included tea, dyes, perfumes, and porcelain; Western exports included horses, camels, honey, wine, and gold. The spread of paper and gunpowder affected political history across Eurasia.

The network was highly decentralized and security was sparse, with threats from bandits, nomadic raiders, and harsh terrain. Few travelers covered its full length, relying instead on middlemen such as the Sogdians. It also carried religious, philosophical, and scientific ideas, especially those of [[Buddhism]], and diseases such as plague, possibly contributing to the [[Black Death]]. From 1453 the [[Ottoman Empire]] competed for control of the overland routes, which prompted European polities to seek alternatives, marking the start of the Age of Discovery. In the 21st century, "New Silk Road" describes large infrastructure projects, including the Chinese [[Belt and Road Initiative]]. UNESCO designated the Chang'an-Tianshan corridor a World Heritage Site in 2014 and the Zarafshan-Karakum Corridor in 2023.

The concept is contested. Some historians prefer "Silk Routes" because it was never a single route, and the term was not used by Marco Polo. Warwick Ball calls it a "myth" of modern academia, arguing that the maritime spice trade mattered more to the Roman economy and that no free overland movement of goods existed before the Mongol Empire. William Dalrymple notes that maritime travel cost only a fifth of overland transport. Critics add that the term privileges the sedentary empires at either end of Eurasia and sidelines steppe nomads, India, and Iran.

[[Chemical element]] (symbol Ag, from Latin *argentum*; atomic number 47), a soft, white, lustrous transition metal.

Silver has the highest electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity, and reflectivity of any metal. It is extremely ductile and malleable, with a density of 10.503 g/cm³, a melting point of 961.8 °C, and a boiling point of 2,162 °C. It resists oxidation in air but tarnishes on exposure to sulfur compounds, forming black silver sulfide. Its electron configuration resembles that of its neighbours in group 11, [[Copper|copper]] and [[Gold|gold]]. Naturally occurring silver consists of two stable isotopes, ¹⁰⁷Ag (51.839%) and ¹⁰⁹Ag, an almost equal abundance that is rare in the periodic table.

Silver occurs as native silver, as an alloy with gold ([[Electrum|electrum]]), and in minerals such as acanthite, argentite, and chlorargyrite. Most is recovered as a byproduct of lead–zinc, copper, and gold mining. World mine production was about 25,300 metric tons in 2024, led by Mexico (6,300 tons), China (3,300 tons), Peru (3,100 tons), and Poland (1,300 tons).

One of the seven metals of antiquity, silver has long been valued as a precious metal and a coinage metal, with an enduring role in monetary systems, jewellery, tableware, and decorative arts. Its purity is measured per mille; a 94%-pure alloy is "0.940 fine". Because pure silver is soft, it is usually alloyed with copper or other metals for jewellery, [[Coin|coinage]], and household objects.

Industrial uses accounted for about 59% of demand in 2024. They include photovoltaics, electrical contacts and conductors, printed electronics, brazing alloys, catalysis, specialised mirrors and window coatings, and antimicrobial materials such as wound dressings. Silver halides are important in photographic film and paper, though digital imaging has reduced demand. Silver is rarely used for its conductivity because of its cost, but during World War II in the U.S., 13,540 tons were used for the electromagnets of calutrons that enriched uranium, because of a wartime shortage of copper.

Venezuelan military officer and statesman who led much of northern and western South America to independence from the [[Spanish Empire]].

Known as El Libertador, "the Liberator", he was born in [[Caracas]] into a wealthy criollo family but lost both parents as a child. He was educated abroad and lived in [[Madrid]] from 1800 to 1802, where he was introduced to Enlightenment philosophy and married María Teresa Rodríguez del Toro y Alaysa, who died of yellow fever in 1803. On a Grand Tour that ended in [[Rome]] in 1805, he swore to end Spanish rule in the Americas. He returned to Venezuela in 1807 and promoted independence among wealthy creoles.

Bolívar began his military career in 1810 as a militia officer in the Venezuelan War of Independence. After Spanish forces subdued New Granada in 1815, he went into exile on [[Jamaica]]. In [[Haiti]], he befriended the revolutionary leader Alexandre Pétion, and after promising to abolish slavery in Spanish America he received military support and returned to Venezuela. He established a third republic in 1817 and in 1819 crossed the [[Andes]] to liberate New Granada. He and his allies defeated the Spanish in Venezuela and Panama in 1821, Ecuador in 1822, Peru in 1824, and Bolivia in 1825. Venezuela, New Granada, Ecuador, and Panama were merged into the Republic of Colombia ([[Gran Colombia]]), with Bolívar as president there and in Peru and Bolivia.

Influenced by Enlightenment ideals and the French Revolution, he pursued republican government but favored strong centralized authority, including a president-for-life in some of his constitutional proposals. His insistence on unitary governance over federalism provoked rebellions from autonomists such as José Antonio Páez. Increasingly disillusioned, he was removed from office step by step, resigned the presidency of Colombia, and died of tuberculosis in 1830. Gran Colombia dissolved by 1831. He is regarded throughout Latin America as a hero and national icon; Bolivia and Venezuela (as the Bolivarian Republic) are named after him.
